About David Hume

David Hume (1711–1776) was the Scottish Enlightenment’s greatest empiricist and skeptical naturalist, author of the Treatise of Human Nature and later Enquiries. Largely denied academic chairs over religious suspicion, he served as librarian and diplomat and wrote a bestselling History of England.

Interpretation

The sentence closes Hume's essay "The Sceptic" (1742), where he has spent pages arguing that philosophical systems have almost no power to change what people feel or how they live. It is not a renunciation of philosophy but a placement of it: reflection is an activity conducted by beings who also have bodies, tempers, tables, and company. Hume's own practice matches the sentence — after skeptical arguments that seem to dissolve everything, he reports dining and backgammon pulling him back, and treats that return as data, not weakness.

Why it matters

It supplies a test for any worldview you are considering: can an actual human live it, on an ordinary Tuesday? A philosophy that requires you to stop being a person to be consistent has, for Hume, disqualified itself rather than you.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Be a philosopher; but amidst all your philosophy,…”?

“Be a philosopher; but amidst all your philosophy,…” comes from The Sceptic, (1742), attributed to David Hume.

What does David Hume mean by human nature?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Aristotle and Blaise Pascal), human nature is framed through Peripatetic School and Christian Existential Precursor. Some passages define human nature; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through human nature, wisdom.
